topic: Cornea gets oxygen directly from the air: avascular cornea, tear film, overnight swelling, sleeping in contacts
hook: Your eyes take oxygen straight from the air

slides.title: Zero blood vessels
slides.body: Your cornea has no blood vessels at all. That's why it's clear enough for light to pass through.
slides.image_prompt: Extreme close-up of a clear glass dome lens catching light, crystal transparent, soft blue background, scientific macro style

slides.title: Fed by your tears
slides.body: Oxygen from the air dissolves into your tear film, then seeps straight into the cornea's cells.
slides.image_prompt: A single glistening water droplet on a curved transparent surface with tiny oxygen bubbles drifting into it, soft morning light

slides.title: Eyes closed at night
slides.body: Asleep, it gets oxygen from vessels in your eyelids instead. It runs so low the cornea swells about 4% by morning.
slides.image_prompt: Dark bedroom at night, moonlight on a pillow, a faint glowing blue dome suggesting a resting eye, calm and quiet mood

slides.title: Why contacts matter
slides.body: Sleeping in contact lenses cuts that supply further. The CDC says it raises eye infection risk up to 8 times.
slides.image_prompt: A contact lens resting on a fingertip-free glass surface beside an open lens case and bedside lamp, night setting, soft shadows

cta: Follow so you never miss the next one
caption:
Your cornea, the clear front window of your eye, has no blood vessels. Instead, it pulls oxygen directly from the air through the thin layer of tears covering it.

At night, with your eyes shut, it has to rely on vessels in your eyelids, and it swells slightly until you wake up. That's also why sleeping in contact lenses is a bad idea: the CDC says it raises your risk of eye infection 6 to 8 times. Sources: CDC, American Academy of Ophthalmology.

Be honest: have you ever fallen asleep with your contacts in? 👀
